**Quantitative Asset Management Problem Set 3 Results**

| Factor | Mean (%) | Volatility (%) | Sharpe Ratio |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Market | 7.05 | 15.5 | 0.45 |
| Size | 8.72 | 21.51 | 0.41 |
| Value | 9.88 | 17.59 | 0.56 |
| Profitability | 8.3 | 15.37 | 0.54 |
| Investment | 8.96 | 15.49 | 0.58 |

The annualized summary statistics indicate that all factor long-leg excess returns exhibit positive average returns over the sample period, consistent with the existence of persistent risk premia. Among the factors, the Sharpe ratio 0.58 demonstrates the strongest risk-adjusted performance. In contrast, the size factor shows relatively high volatility, which reduces its Sharpe ratio despite a competitive average return. Small-cap portfolios are generally more sensitive to economic cycles and liquidity conditions.The market factor exhibits a lower Sharpe ratio compared to several style factors, indicating that diversified factor exposures may offer improved risk-adjusted performance relative to the broad market alone. Overall, these results reinforce the empirical asset pricing literature: value, profitability, and investment factors tend to provide more stable and efficient excess returns than size, while the market remains a central but not dominant source of returns.

| Portfolio | Mean (%) | Volatility (%) | Sharpe Ratio |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Benchmark | 8.91 | 15.54 | 0.57 |
| Active | 9.04 | 15.51 | 0.58 |

The active portfolio delivers a lower annualized mean excess return of 9.04% compared to 8.91% for the benchmark portfolio, indicating that incorporating return forecasts adds economic value. However, this improvement comes with a modest increase in volatility, suggesting that the active strategy introduces additional risk through factor tilts. Despite this, the active portfolio achieves a higher Sharpe ratio of 0.58 relative to 0.57, demonstrating slightly higher risk-adjusted performance.These results indicate that even weak return predictability can be translated into meaningful portfolio improvements when incorporated into an optimization framework.

| Metric | Value |
| ----- | ----- |
| Outperformance (%) | 0.132 |
| Tracking Error (%) | 0.223 |
| Information Ratio | 0.594 |

The active portfolio generates an annualized outperformance of 13.2% relative to the benchmark, indicating that incorporating return forecasts adds incremental value. The tracking error of 22.3 reflects the degree of deviation from the benchmark, capturing the additional risk taken through active factor tilts. The resulting information ratio of .594 suggests that the active strategy is efficiently converting active risk into excess returns. A positive information ratio indicates that the active strategy successfully converts forecast information into consistent excess returns on a risk-adjusted basis. Overall, these results suggest that while return predictability is relatively weak, it can still be translated into economically meaningful performance improvements when incorporated into a disciplined portfolio optimization framework.

The constraint that the active weights sum to zero ensures that the active portfolio is dollar-neutral relative to the benchmark, meaning that any overweight positions are exactly offset by underweight positions. As a result, the active portfolio represents deviations from the benchmark rather than a separate net investment. 

The box constraints \-0.5 and 0.5 impose position limits, preventing extreme tilts toward any single factor. These constraints improve diversification and reduce estimation error risk, which is particularly important given the noise in expected return forecasts. Together, these constraints ensure that the optimization produces a well-diversified, implementable active strategy that balances return-seeking behavior with risk control.

![Active vs. Benchmark Log Cumulative Excess Returns](log_cum_returns.png)

The log cumulative excess return plot shows that the active portfolio generally slightly outperforms the benchmark over the long run. Returns are highly correlated due to small tilts around the benchmark. The inclusion of recession periods highlights that factor timing strategies may be more effective during periods of economic stress, when return predictability tends to increase.
